nameStory: The "crevalle" in this fish's name comes from the Spanish word "caballa," meaning horse mackerel, which sailors later corrupted to "cavalli" and then "crevalle." The "jack" part refers to its membership in the jack family, where many species share this common name. Over time, this powerful fish picked up many nicknames including "common jack" and "yellow cavalli," reflecting its widespread distribution and the golden hues that often tint its silvery body.
description: The Atlantic Crevalle Jack is a powerful, deep-bodied fish with a distinctly compressed, oval shape that cuts through the water like a living torpedo. These silvery predators typically grow to about 2 feet long in New England waters, though they can reach over 4 feet in southern waters. Their metallic silver sides often show golden or yellowish tints, and they're built for speed with a narrow tail base and deeply forked tail fin. You'll recognize them by their steep, blunt head profile and the way they move in quick, aggressive bursts.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, compressed oval body that feels firm and muscular to the touch, with a steep, blunt forehead that drops almost vertically from the top of the head to the mouth

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Deeply forked tail fin with a very narrow base where it connects to the body, and a distinctive black spot on the rear edge of the gill cover that's visible even on dead fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright metallic silver sides with a darker blue-green back, often showing golden or brassy tints, especially around the head and shoulders

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large terminal mouth that opens at the front tip of the snout, filled with small, sharp teeth that feel like fine sandpaper when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: In New England waters, typically 12-24 inches long and weighing 2-8 pounds, with a solid, dense feel that's heavier than you'd expect for their size

habitat: Atlantic Crevalle Jacks are visitors to New England's warmer coastal waters, typically found in bays, harbors, and nearshore areas during summer months. They prefer areas with structure like rocky reefs, pier pilings, or jetties where smaller fish congregate, and you might spot them in estuaries where rivers meet the sea. These warm-water fish rarely venture into waters deeper than 100 feet in our region, staying close to shore where the water temperature stays above their tolerance threshold.

seasonality.spring: Crevalle jacks begin arriving in southern New England waters as temperatures warm, usually appearing first around Cape Cod and the Islands in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for crevalle jacks in New England, when they're most active and numerous in bays, harbors, and nearshore waters, often seen hunting in schools.
seasonality.fall: As water temperatures drop, crevalle jacks become increasingly urgent about feeding and begin their migration south, making this a good time for anglers but numbers decline rapidly.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to avoid fatal cold temperatures, though stragglers that fail to migrate may be found dead or dying.

funFact: Crevalle jacks that get trapped in New England's cooling fall waters face a dramatic race against time—they must migrate south before water temperatures drop below their survival threshold, or they'll literally freeze to death in mass die-offs that can wash hundreds of fish onto beaches.
confusionNotes: Crevalle jacks are most often confused with bluefish due to their similar size and aggressive feeding behavior, but crevalle jacks have a much deeper, more compressed body profile while bluefish are more torpedo-shaped. Remember: "Crevalle is compressed, bluefish is bullet-shaped."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Atlantic" Crevalle Jack, this is the same species found in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean—the name simply distinguishes it from Pacific jack species. Many anglers don't realize these are warm-water visitors to New England, not year-round residents, which explains their sporadic appearances.
compareHints: Compared to its close relatives, the Blue Runner has a more elongated body and lacks the crevalle jack's steep forehead profile, while the Yellow Jack (rare in New England) is more golden overall and has a less compressed body shape. The crevalle jack's distinctly deep, oval profile and blunt head make it the most robust-looking of the three jacks you might encounter in our waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, the blue runner is distinguished by its prominent blue stripe - crevalle jacks lack this blue coloration and have a more golden appearance with a black gill spot, while yellow jacks are, as their name suggests, more yellow overall.
Compared to the more common crevalle jack, yellow jacks have a more golden coloration and longer jaw that extends past the eye.
